title: Statistical Advantage of Softmax Attention: Insights from Single-Location Regression
claim: Softmax attention consistently outperforms alternative architectures on retrieval tasks, yet all architectures perform similarly on general linguistic proficiency tasks.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, line plots vs model size, shared legends in-panel
description: Two line plots share an x-axis of model size, from 70M to 7B parameters. Panel (a) shows retrieval accuracy on Needle-in-a-Haystack. Colors mark context lengths of 2k, 4k and 8k, plus the average in red. Line style marks the architecture: LLaMA (softmax) is thick and solid, and TNL, HGRN2 and cos2 are thin dashed or dotted lines. The thick LLaMA curves jump to near 100% accuracy at 410M, while the alternatives stay far lower, mostly below 50%. Panel (b) shows normalized linguistic proficiency metrics, such as CSR, WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity, and SCROLLS. All architectures rise together and cluster tightly toward 1.0. The shaded gridded backgrounds, in-plot legends and captions below each panel make the contrast between the panels the main message.
caption: (Shen et al., 2024, Tables 4 and 11): Comparison of softmax Transformer (LLaMA, bolded line) with kernelized attention (TNL, cos2) and state-space models (HGRN2), as a function of the model size, and for various tasks (retrieval tasks on the left, linguistic proficiency on the right). All architectures have similar performance for the linguistic proficiency tasks, whereas in retrieval tasks the softmax attention systematically outperforms alternatives.
abstract: Large language models rely on attention mechanisms with a softmax activation. Yet the dominance of softmax over alternatives (e.g., component-wise or linear) remains poorly understood, and many theoretical works have focused on the easier-to-analyze linearized attention. In this work, we address this gap through a principled study of the single-location regression task, where the output depends on a linear transformation of a single input token at a random location. Building on ideas from statistical physics, we develop an analysis of attention-based predictors in the high-dimensional limit, where generalization performance is captured by a small set of order parameters. At the population level, we show that softmax achieves the Bayes risk, whereas linear attention fundamentally falls short. We then examine other activation functions to identify which properties are necessary for optimal performance. Finally, we analyze the finite-sample regime: we provide an asymptotic characterization of the test error and show that, while softmax is no longer Bayes-optimal, it consistently outperforms linear attention. We discuss the connection with optimization by gradient-based algorithms.
